lessons.title: Determining Optimal Planting Date
lessons.body:
In soybean farming, the day you plant is the single biggest factor you control that decides your yield. Plant too early and seeds rot in cold, wet soil or seedlings get killed by late frost. Plant too late and your crop runs out of water during pod fill, or gets hit by early frost before maturity. The goal is to have flowering and pod fill happen when there is plenty of sunlight and rain, and to finish before the dry season or cold sets in.

Start by knowing your local rainy season. In most of West Africa, the best planting window is from late June to mid-July, once rains have settled and the soil is consistently moist to a depth of 15 cm. In East Africa, the long rains (MarchâMay) and short rains (OctoberâDecember) dictate planting. For example, in Uganda, plant with the first reliable rains in late March or early April. In southern Africa, planting from mid-November to mid-December is common. Always check with your local extension officer for the exact window in your area.

Soil temperature matters. Soybean seeds germinate best when soil at 5 cm depth is at least 15Â°C and rising. You can measure this with a simple soil thermometer. If you plant when soil is colder, emergence will be slow and uneven, and seeds may be attacked by soil fungi. Also, avoid planting right before a heavy downpourâcrusting can prevent seedlings from breaking through.

A practical rule: plant when you have had at least 20â25 mm of rain over 2â3 days and the forecast shows more rain coming. If you have irrigation, you can plant a bit earlier, but you must keep the soil moist until emergence. Remember, soybean is a short-day plant; late planting shortens the growing period and reduces yield. So donât delay once conditions are right.

Finally, stagger planting if you have a large field. Plant a portion, then wait 5â7 days and plant more. This spreads risk from drought or pests and spreads your harvest labour. Keep records of planting dates and yields each year to fine-tune your own optimal date.

lessons.title: Seedbed Preparation and Planting Depth
lessons.body:
A good seedbed gives soybean seeds the best start. Soybean needs a fine, firm, and level seedbed with no large clods or crop residues that block emergence. Poor seedbed preparation leads to poor seed-to-soil contact, uneven germination, and lower yields. Start preparing early, before the rains, so you can plant as soon as the soil is ready.

First, clear the field of previous crop residues and weeds. You can use a hand hoe, ox-drawn plough, or tractor. If you use a plough, follow with a harrow to break clods and level the soil. In conservation agriculture, you can plant directly into residue with a jab planter or no-till drill, but ensure the residue is not too thick. Aim for a seedbed that is loose to about 15 cm depth, with the top 5 cm fine and firm. A simple test: press your finger into the soilâit should sink about 2â3 cm with moderate pressure.

Planting depth is critical. The ideal depth is 3â5 cm (about 1.5â2 inches). If you plant shallower than 3 cm, the seed may dry out or be eaten by birds. If you plant deeper than 5 cm, the seedling uses too much energy to reach the surface, and emergence is poor, especially in heavy soils. In sandy soils, plant slightly deeper (up to 5 cm) because they dry out faster. In clay soils, plant shallower (3â4 cm) to avoid crusting.

To achieve uniform depth, use a planting stick, jab planter, or seed drill with depth control. If planting by hand, make a furrow with a hoe to a consistent depth, drop seeds 5â8 cm apart, then cover with soil and press lightly. Do not leave air pockets. After planting, if the soil is dry, water lightly if you have irrigation, or wait for rain. Avoid walking over the planted rows, as this compacts the soil.

Finally, ensure the seedbed is free of weeds before planting. Weeds compete for water and nutrients. You can pre-irrigate to germinate weeds, then shallowly cultivate before planting. A well-prepared seedbed can increase germination by 20â30% and set you up for a healthy crop.

lessons.title: Row Spacing and Plant Population Density
lessons.body:
Soybean yield depends on how many healthy plants you have per hectare and how well they capture sunlight. Row spacing and plant population are tools you can adjust to maximise yield. The goal is to achieve a uniform stand with enough plants to shade out weeds and produce many pods, but not so dense that plants compete for water and nutrients.

Recommended row spacing for soybean in Africa varies. In many regions, 50â75 cm between rows is common. For example, in Nigeria, 75 cm rows are typical, while in Zambia, 45â50 cm rows are used for higher yields. Narrower rows (40â50 cm) often yield more because they close the canopy faster, reducing weed growth and increasing light interception. However, you need to ensure your equipment can handle the spacing. If you plant by hand, you can use a string to mark rows.

Within the row, aim for 5â10 cm between plants. This gives a final plant population of about 250,000 to 400,000 plants per hectare. For 75 cm rows, you need about 4â6 plants per metre of row. For 50 cm rows, about 6â8 plants per metre. A simple calculation: if you want 300,000 plants/ha and your rows are 75 cm apart, then each metre of row should have 300,000 / (10,000/0.75) = 22.5 plants per metre? Wait, thatâs wrong. Letâs do it properly: 1 hectare = 10,000 mÂ². With 75 cm (0.75 m) rows, total row length per hectare = 10,000 / 0.75 = 13,333 m. To get 300,000 plants, you need 300,000 / 13,333 = 22.5 plants per metre? Thatâs too high. Actually, soybean plants are spaced about 5â10 cm apart, so 10â20 plants per metre. But that would give 133,330 to 266,660 plants per hectare. So typical target is 250,000â400,000 plants/ha. For 75 cm rows, 4â6 plants per metre gives 53,333â80,000 plants/ha? Thatâs too low. Letâs recalc: 13,333 m of row per ha. If you have 4 plants per metre, thatâs 53,332 plants/ha. Thatâs too low. Actually, for soybean, you want about 30â40 plants per square metre? No. Letâs use standard: 50 cm rows, 5 cm spacing: 10,000 / 0.5 = 20,000 m row length. 20,000 m * (100 cm / 5 cm) = 20,000 * 20 = 400,000 plants/ha. So for 50 cm rows, 5 cm spacing gives 400,000 plants/ha. For 75 cm rows, 5 cm spacing gives 10,000/0.75=13,333 m; 13,333 * 20 = 266,660 plants/ha. So thatâs fine. So 5 cm spacing is good. So target 250,000â400,000 plants/ha.

To achieve this, calibrate your seed drop. If you plant by hand, drop 2â3 seeds per hole at 5 cm spacing, then thin to one plant per stand after emergence. Overplanting and thinning is better than underplanting. After emergence, count plants in a few 1 mÂ² areas to check your population. If itâs too low, consider replanting. If too high, thin to reduce competition. Proper spacing and population set the foundation for a high-yielding soybean crop.

lessons.title: Seed Treatment and Inoculation
lessons.body:
Seed treatment and inoculation are two cheap steps that can boost soybean yields significantly. Soybean seeds are vulnerable to soil-borne diseases and insects after planting. Also, soybean needs nitrogen-fixing bacteria (rhizobia) in the soil to convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use. If you have never grown soybean in your field, or itâs been more than 3â4 years, you need to inoculate.

First, seed treatment. Treat seeds with a fungicide and insecticide before planting. Common fungicides include thiram or captan, and insecticides like imidacloprid. These protect against damping-off, seed rot, and early insect damage. You can buy pre-treated seeds, or treat yourself. Follow label instructions carefullyâoverdosing can harm the seed. Mix the seed with the chemical in a bucket or plastic bag, ensuring even coating. Wear gloves and a mask. Treated seed should be planted within a few days; donât store it long.

Second, inoculation. Rhizobium inoculant is a powder or liquid containing live bacteria. It is specific to soybean, so ask for soybean inoculant. You can buy it from agro-dealers. To apply, mix the inoculant with a sticker (like a sugar solution or commercial sticker) and coat the seeds evenly. Use about 5â10 g of inoculant per kg of seed. Do this in a shaded area, away from direct sunlight, because UV light kills the bacteria. Plant immediately after inoculationâwithin 24 hours. Donât mix inoculant with fungicide simultaneously; it can kill the bacteria. If you must use both, apply fungicide first, let it dry, then apply inoculant just before planting.

If you have grown soybean in the same field successfully before, you may not need to inoculate every year, but itâs good practice to inoculate every 2â3 years. Also, if your soil is very acidic (pH below 5.5), rhizobia may not survive. Apply lime to raise pH to 6.0â6.5. Inoculation can increase yields by 10â30% and reduces the need for nitrogen fertiliser. Itâs a low-cost, high-return investment.

Finally, store inoculant in a cool, dry place and check the expiry date. Never expose it to high heat. Proper seed treatment and inoculation give your crop a strong start and healthier plants.

lessons.title: Calibrating Planting Equipment
lessons.body:
Calibrating your planting equipment ensures you drop the right amount of seed at the correct spacing and depth. Whether you use a hand jab planter, ox-drawn planter, or tractor-mounted seed drill, calibration saves seed, money, and gives you a uniform stand. An uncalibrated planter can waste 20â30% of your seed and lead to poor yields.

Start by checking the seed meter or plate. For plate planters, select the correct plate for soybean seed size. Soybean seeds are larger than maize or sorghum, so use a plate with larger cells. If the plate is wrong, seeds may be cracked or multiple seeds dropped per cell. For drill planters, adjust the seed rate setting according to the manual. A good target is 50â60 kg of seed per hectare for small-seeded varieties, or 70â80 kg for larger seeds. But always follow the recommended seeding rate for your variety.

To calibrate, first measure a known distance, say 50 metres, in the field. Fill the hopper with seed. Mark the starting point. Push or drive the planter over the 50 m at your normal speed. Then collect and weigh the seed dropped over that distance. Calculate the seed rate per hectare: (seed weight in kg / 50 m) * 10,000 mÂ² / row spacing in m. For example, if you drop 0.3 kg over 50 m with 0.75 m rows, then per hectare: (0.3/50)*10,000/0.75 = 80 kg/ha. Adjust the setting until you get the desired rate. Repeat 2â3 times and take the average.

Also check depth control. Plant a few seeds and dig them up to see if they are at 3â5 cm. Adjust the depth wheels or press wheels. For hand jab planters, check that the mechanism drops 2â3 seeds per jab and that you can maintain 5 cm spacing. You might need to practise on a small area. For tractor planters, check tyre pressure and ground speed; too fast can cause skips.

Finally, clean and lubricate your planter after use. Replace worn parts. Calibrate every season and whenever you change seed lot or variety. A well-calibrated planter is the difference between a uniform, high-yielding field and a patchy, low-yielding one.

lessons.title: Replanting Decisions and Strategies
lessons.body:
Sometimes, despite your best efforts, the first planting fails. You may have poor emergence due to drought, crusting, insects, or disease. Replanting is a tough decision because it costs extra seed, labour, and time. But if the stand is too thin, replanting can be more profitable than keeping a poor crop. Hereâs how to decide.

First, assess the stand. Wait until the crop is at least 10â14 days old. Count plants in several 1 mÂ² areas across the field. If you have less than 50% of the recommended population (e.g., less than 125,000 plants/ha when you aimed for 250,000), replanting is usually worthwhile. If you have 50â75% stand, you might consider patchingâreplanting only the bare spots. If above 75%, keep the crop; soybean can compensate by branching and producing more pods per plant.

Next, consider the cause. If the problem is drought, wait for rain. If the soil is crusted, a light harrow or rake can help seedlings emerge. If insects or diseases are the issue, you must treat the seed or soil before replanting, or youâll lose the new crop too. If the cause is poor seed or planting depth, correct that. Replanting into the same problem is a waste.

Timing is critical. If you replant too late, the crop may not mature before the end of the rains or before frost. Check the maturity days of your variety. If you have at least 90â100 days of growing season left, you can replant. If not, consider a shorter-maturity variety. In some cases, you might switch to another crop like cowpea or maize if time is too short.

When replanting, use fresh, treated, and inoculated seed. Prepare the seedbed again if needed. You may need to increase seed rate slightly to compensate for expected losses. After replanting, monitor closely for pests and weeds. Replanting can still give you 70â80% of a normal yield if done early and correctly. Donât delay the decisionâthe sooner you replant, the better your chances.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil temperature at 5 cm depth for soybean germination?
quiz.explanation: Soybean seeds germinate best when soil temperature is at least 15Â°C and rising.

quiz.q: In West Africa, what is the typical optimal planting window for soybean?
quiz.explanation: In West Africa, the best planting window is from late June to mid-July once rains have settled.

quiz.q: How much rain over 2â3 days is a good indicator to plant soybean?
quiz.explanation: At least 20â25 mm of rain over 2â3 days with more forecast is a practical planting trigger.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid planting soybean right before a heavy downpour?
options: A) Seeds will germinate too fast
B) Soil crusting can prevent seedling emergence
quiz.explanation: Heavy rain can cause soil crusting, which makes it hard for seedlings to break through the surface.

quiz.q: What is the ideal planting depth for soybean?
quiz.explanation: The ideal planting depth is 3â5 cm for good emergence and moisture access.

quiz.q: In sandy soils, soybean should be planted:
options: C) Slightly deeper, up to 5 cm
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils dry out faster, so planting slightly deeper (up to 5 cm) helps ensure moisture for germination.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check if the seedbed is firm enough?
options: A) Press your finger into the soil; it should sink 2â3 cm with moderate pressure
B) Drop a seed; it should bounce
C) Step on the soil; it should not leave a footprint
D) Pour water; it should drain immediately
quiz.explanation: Pressing a finger into the soil and having it sink 2â3 cm indicates good firmness for planting.

quiz.q: Why is a fine, level seedbed important for soybean?
options: B) It ensures good seed-to-soil contact and uniform emergence
quiz.explanation: A fine, level seedbed provides good seed-to-soil contact, leading to uniform germination and emergence.

quiz.q: What is a common row spacing for soybean in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Row spacing of 50â75 cm is common, with narrower rows often yielding more.

quiz.q: What is the recommended plant population density for soybean?
quiz.explanation: Aim for 250,000â400,000 plants per hectare for optimal yield.

quiz.q: If you plant in 75 cm rows, what in-row spacing gives about 300,000 plants/ha?
quiz.explanation: With 75 cm rows, 5 cm spacing gives approximately 266,660 plants/ha, close to the target.

quiz.q: Why are narrower rows (40â50 cm) often better for soybean?
options: A) They allow more air circulation
B) They close the canopy faster, reducing weeds
quiz.explanation: Narrower rows close the canopy faster, which shades out weeds and increases light interception.

quiz.q: What should you do if your soybean stand is too dense?
options: A) Leave it; it will self-thin
quiz.explanation: Thinning reduces competition for water and nutrients, leading to healthier plants.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of seed treatment with fungicide and insecticide?
options: B) To protect against soil-borne diseases and insects
quiz.explanation: Seed treatment protects seeds and seedlings from damping-off, seed rot, and early insect damage.

quiz.q: What type of inoculant is needed for soybean?
quiz.explanation: Soybean requires specific Rhizobium bacteria for nitrogen fixation.

quiz.q: How should you apply inoculant to soybean seeds?
options: A) Mix with fungicide and apply together
B) Coat seeds evenly in a shaded area and plant within 24 hours
D) Sprinkle on soil after planting
quiz.explanation: Inoculant should be coated evenly on seeds in shade and planted within 24 hours to keep bacteria alive.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of inoculant per kg of seed?
quiz.explanation: Use about 5â10 g of inoculant per kg of seed for effective inoculation.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing inoculant with fungicide at the same time?
options: A) It causes seeds to stick together
B) Fungicide can kill the rhizobia bacteria
quiz.explanation: Fungicides can kill the live rhizobia bacteria, so apply them separately.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calibrating a planting equipment?
options: A) Fill the hopper with seed
B) Check the seed meter or plate for correct size
quiz.explanation: Checking the seed meter or plate ensures the correct seed size and drop mechanism.

quiz.q: What is a good target seed rate for soybean per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Seed rate varies with seed size, but 50â60 kg/ha for small seeds and 70â80 kg/ha for larger seeds is typical.

quiz.q: How can you calculate the seed rate per hectare after a calibration run?
quiz.explanation: The formula (seed weight in kg / distance in m) * 10,000 mÂ² / row spacing in m gives kg/ha.

quiz.q: What should you check after calibrating seed drop?
quiz.explanation: After calibrating seed drop, check that planting depth is 3â5 cm.

quiz.q: How often should you calibrate your planter?
options: B) Every season and when changing seed lot
C) Only when buying new equipment
quiz.explanation: Calibrate every season and whenever you change seed lot or variety to ensure accuracy.

quiz.q: When should you consider replanting soybean?
options: A) When stand is less than 50% of recommended population
B) When stand is 80% of recommended
C) When plants are 30 days old
D) When it rains after planting
quiz.explanation: If stand is below 50% of the target population, replanting is usually worthwhile.

quiz.q: What is patching in the context of replanting?
options: B) Replanting only the bare spots
C) Adding fertiliser to weak spots
quiz.explanation: Patching means replanting only the areas with poor emergence, saving seed and labour.

quiz.q: If you have 60% stand, what is the recommended action?
quiz.explanation: With 50â75% stand, patching bare spots is often sufficient.

quiz.q: What should you check before deciding to replant?
options: A) The cause of poor emergence
B) The colour of the soil
C) The phase of the moon
quiz.explanation: Identifying the cause (e.g., drought, crusting, pests) helps correct it before replanting.

quiz.q: How many growing days do you need left to successfully replant soybean?
quiz.explanation: You need at least 90â100 days of growing season left for the replanted crop to mature.

quiz.q: What should you use when replanting?
options: B) Fresh, treated, and inoculated seed
quiz.explanation: Use fresh, treated, and inoculated seed to give the new crop the best start.

quiz.q: What is a potential outcome if you replant early and correctly?
quiz.explanation: Replanting early and correctly can still give 70â80% of a normal yield.
